reviewer_comments.reviewer_4: We thank all the reviewers for their positive feedback about the significance of the work and their critical comments that have greatly helped us improve the quality of our manuscript and distinguish the contributions of this manuscript over the previously existing literature. A point-by-point response to the reviewer comments is below in blue. REVIEWER COMMENTS Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author): This manuscript provides a detailed structural analysis of the bridge helix (BH) in Cas12a activation, offering insights into its role in allosteric regulation. The cryoEM data are well-analyzed, and the findings contribute meaningfully to the understanding of Cas12a’s conformational transitions. The study is of interest to researchers in CRISPR biology and genome editing. While the manuscript is generally well- prepared, some points require further clarification and discussion to strengthen the conclusions. We thank the reviewer for the positive feedback about the significance of the work and the quality of cryo-EM data analysis and its contribution to understanding the role of BH in Cas12a’s activation. Points which needed further clarification are addressed in the revision as described below. Major Comments 1. The study suggests that BH’s loop-to-helical transition directly influences RuvC activation. However, it remains unclear whether this is a cause or a consequence of R-loop formation. Additional discussion, or reference to supporting biochemical evidence, would help clarify this point. To clarify whether BH’s loop-to-helical transition is a cause or a consequence of R-loop formation and its influence on RuvC activation, we have conducted additional biochemical, structural, and computational analyzes. The results now clearly establish that BH’s loop-to-helical transition is a cause since without this transition, R-loop formation is inhibited mid-way through, and the formation of the helical structure of the hybrid is impaired. We also show that, with a variant able to undergo the loop-to- helical transition, BH–RuvC-lid interactions are only secondary as the variants maintain efficient on- target DNA cleavage without the BH–RuvC-lid interactions. 1 Biochemical Analysis: To probe the allosteric mechanism, residues that mediate BH-lid interactions to convert the lid from a loop to a helical form at different stages of the activation process, thereby mediating the exposure of RuvC active site, were identified based on wild-type (FnoCas12aWT) and BH-variant (FnoCas12aKD2P) structures. Residues R964 of the BH and E1020 and K1021 of the RuvC-lid were substituted with alanine, along with a double variant E1020A/K1021A in both FnoCas12aWT and FnoCas12aKD2P backgrounds. In vitro plasmid DNA cleavage assays using both matched (MCH) and mismatched (MM) DNA substrates (MM2, PAM proximal mismatch and MM13, mid R-loop mismatch) were performed to assess the effects of the alanine substitutions. In the FnoCas12aWT background, single substitutions do not show prominent impairments, except for MM13-R964A combination, consistent with the stabilizing effect that the BH offers for the allosteric interactions. On the other hand, in the FnoCas12aKD2P background, where BH stability is impaired by the proline substitutions, the substitutions at R964 of the BH and the double variant (E1020/K1021) of the RuvC-lid, impacted both TS and NTS cleavages. In comparison, the only significant impact seen in FnoCas12aWT is the accumulation of nicked intermediate in R964A-MM13 combination (Figures 3e-f, Supplementary Figs.17,18, and Supplementary Table 11). These data clearly show that DNA cleavage is an additive process with combinations from effects from the BH’s loop-to-helical transition, opening of the RuvC active site by the helical transition of the lid, and the strength of complementary pairing between the RNA and DNA. Of these three, BH’s transition has the most significant contribution since in the wild-type backbone, all substitutions show minimal effect, except in R964-MM13, which indicates that the second contributor is the strength of complementary base pairing that is also dictated by the position of the mismatch between the RNA and DNA. The new results are presented in pages 12-15, with a summary in pages 14 (lines 23-26, and 15 (lines 1-10) which is copied below. “Our findings show that contacts between the BH and RuvC-lid (R964-E1020, E961-K1021) are only secondary to the BH’s helical transition for orchestrating the conformational transitions required for double-strand cleavage and mismatch sensitivity. The wild-type protein with an intact conformational change in the BH can linearize (i.e., both NTS and TS cleavages) despite disrupting the BH–RuvC-lid interactions, with the only significant reduction being in the second strand cleavage for MM13 substrate (Supplementary Fig. 17 and Supplementary Table 11). On the contrary, when BH’s sturdiness is restricted, as in the FnoCas12aKD2P variant, the enzyme becomes highly dependent on these interactions to provide RuvC active site access to ssDNA. In the FnoCas12aKD2P background, while R964A and E1020A/K1021A substitutions impair both strand cleavages, single substitutions (E1020A or K1021A) impede second-strand cleavage (Supplementary Fig. 18a and Supplementary Table 11). These 2 results demonstrate that the BH’s loop-to-helical transition is an allosteric switch coupling R-loop propagation to catalysis and point to the importance of the helicity of the BH in assisting the passage of TS DNA into the RuvC active site pocket. BH, RuvC-H1, and RuvC-lid are potential engineering sites to reduce mismatch tolerance in Cas12a.” Structural Analysis: Structural analysis showed that R964 and R968 interact with nucleotides dG(-7), dT(-8), and U10 of crRNA/DNA in state I4 of FnoCas12aWT (Supplementary Fig.15), while the corresponding interaction is absent in FnoCas12aKD2P (a maximum of 11 base pairs is visible in State 4a). While position 11 of crRNA and TS DNA move closer to the BH in FnoCas12aWT, this interaction stays at around 20 Å FnoCas12aKD2P. Previous studies have shown that 16 nucleotides of base pairing of crRNA and DNA is a checkpoint for Cas12a activation (Stella et al., 2018 and Strohkendl et al., 2024). Thus, it appears that BH’s transition is essential for R-loop propagation, making BH’s transition the cause for R-loop propagation, especially past 10-nucleotides of base pairing. The bending of BH towards R-loop and latching into REC2 domain in parallel with the growing RNA-DNA hybrid appears to give the RNA-DNA hybrid a double-helical structure, implicating the importance of BH in R-loop propagation and stability. This stable configuration of the BH and the R-loop seems to facilitate a concomitant opening of the RuvC active pocket through RuvC-lid remodeling. These points have been added to the Discussion section (page 19 (lines 14-26), which is copied below). “In addition, the elongation of the BH due to the addition of the new helical turns and its bending towards the RNA-DNA hybrid appears to be critical in providing an anchorage for R-loop and to complete the RNA-DNA hybrid formation. In the FnoCas12aWT structures, states I2 and I320 have BH in a loop state prior to its the helical conversion. In these structures, BH is at a distance of 17 Å from the RNA-DNA hybrid with a total of 8-nucleotides of base pairing between the crRNA-guide and TS DNA. In comparison, in state I4, we see a fully formed and bent BH that is closer to the RNA-DNA hybrid (6 Å). In FnoCas12aKD2P, which is not capable of undergoing the loop-to-helical transition, we only see up to a maximum of 11-nucleotides of base pairing between the crRNA-guide and TS DNA, with a distance of ~20 Å from the BH. Interestingly, we also see stacking and distortion of bases towards the end of the R- loop, implicating that the strands are not aligned well with an impaired BH, hinting at the essentiality of the stability provided by the BH in these intermediary stages to drive R-loop propagation. The slowing down of the structural transitions is supported by the lower reaction kinetics of FnoCas12aKD2P when compared to FnoCas12aWT14..” 3 Computational Studies: ⁠Our MD simulations indicate that the BH’s loop-to-helical transition actively shapes the conformational landscape of Cas12a by exerting allosteric influence over the RuvC-lid, crRNA, and DNA. Cross- correlation analyses show a shift from anti-correlated to positively correlated interactions across states, such as S2 to S4b to I4 (especially for nucleotides at position 6 and 8 of crRNA and -8 to -4 of DNA). This reorganization coincides only with the helical transition of the BH, which in turn facilitates the emergence of strong BH–crRNA, BH–DNA, and BH–RuvC-lid couplings in the pre-catalytic state. Overall, these data show that BH’s helical transition is an activating trigger regulating R-loop propagation and opening of RuvC active site pocket (Points have been added in the Results section, page 16 (lines 8-24), which is copied below, and Supplementary Methods 3). “To delineate potential allosteric communication between BH and nucleic acid, we performed correlation analyses of the residues E961, R964, R968, K981, E1020, K1021, and N1022 of the BH, RuvC-H1, and RuvC-lid, as well as nucleotides in crRNA and DNA (Fig. 4c-e). The complete correlation analysis is available in Supplementary Methods 3. Results reveal that BH–RuvC-H1 and RuvC-lid conformations exhibit strongly correlated motions with those of the crRNA and DNA, and that the motions are different between the different states. FnoCas12aKD2P S2 has fewer correlated motions (i.e., components move in the same direction) between the BH–RuvC-H1 and RuvC-lid, while there are several anti-correlated motions (i.e., components move in the opposite direction) between BH–RuvC-H1 and the RNA and DNA (Fig. 4c). In the intermediate state S4b, however, this correlation pattern shifts; there is an increase in the correlated motions between BH–RuvC-H1 and RuvC-lid and a few new motions with the crRNA, while there still is a substantial number of anti-correlated motions with crRNA and DNA (Fig. 4d). In I420 of FnoCas12aWT, we see only correlated motions between BH–RuvC-H1, RuvC-lid, crRNA, and DNA (Fig. 4e). Interestingly, some of the interactions with crRNA and DNA include nucleotides near the middle of the R-loop (~8) providing mechanistic clues on why mismatches between the crRNA and DNA in the R-loop away from the PAM are particularly sensitive in FnoCas12a. This reorganization of the correlation network in different states of the protein points to the pivotal role that the BH–RuvC-H1 transitions play in organizing the cleavage-competent form of Cas12a.” 2. The manuscript suggests that the impaired BH prevents trans-cleavage, but no direct biochemical validation is provided. If prior studies have addressed this, a more explicit reference would be beneficial. Otherwise, acknowledging this limitation would improve clarity. 4 We thank the reviewer for this helpful comment. While the current manuscript focuses on providing structural insights into the cis DNA cleavage mechanism of FnoCas12aKD2P, previous biochemical evidence from our group (Parameshwaran et al., 2021) reported that this variant has significantly reduced trans-cleavage efficiency compared to FnoCas12aWT). We now cite and discuss this study more explicitly in the discussion section to show that the BH transition and the corresponding allosteric activation of RNA/DNA/RuvC-lid are important for trans DNA cleavage as well. We have carefully worded the text to make it clearer to a reader that trans cleavage assay was done in our prior work and that the structural data provides the mechanistic framework that explains the previously observed defect (Points have been added in the Discussion section, page 21, lines 1-9, which is copied below). “In our previous work, we have also demonstrated that FnoCas12aKD2P has a lower trans-cleavage efficiency (0% substrate left for FnoCas12aWT at 5 minutes, compared to 40% remaining in FnoCas12aKD2P after two hours)14. Unlike FnoCas12aWT, which rapidly degraded substrates, FnoCas12aKD2P accumulated linear intermediates and failed to sustain a robust progressive trans- cleavage14. Additionally, FnoCas12aKD2P was unable to perform trans-cleavage when activated by a dsDNA14. The trans-cleavage occurs through keeping the RuvC domain “open” for non-specific ssDNA to access the active site24,53. These observations highlight that impairment of the BH’s helical transition likely blocks the prolonged activated form of the RuvC pocket, preventing trans-cleavage in FnoCas12aKD2P.” 3. The role of BH in Cas12a is emphasized, but how this differs from Cas9 remains unclear. Since Cas9 does not require a major RuvC conformational shift, a brief discussion on this evolutionary divergence would add depth to the paper. We thank the reviewer for this comment. It prompted us to include Cas9 proteins in our structural analyses. Further analyses by including the available structures of Cas9 subtypes (II-A, II-B and II-C) in using the pairwise 3D structural comparison of the BH-RuvC domain of FnoCas12a and various Cas12 subtypes (Fig. 5 and Supplementary Fig. 22) suggest that the Cas9 BH do not align completely with that of FnoCas12a, whereas a helix in the RuvC motif-II is structurally positioned in a similar arrangement as the RuvC-H1 of Cas12a. As the BH and the RuvC motif-II are placed farther away from each other due to the insertion of the REC lobe in between in Cas9, it may not be feasible to translate or couple the conformational changes in the BH to the RuvC motif-II’s helix or vice versa, similar to the coordinated transitions that we observe in Cas12a’s BH and H1 (Supplementary Fig. 23). In Cas12a, the BH and the RuvC-H1 of the RuvC motif-II are located close to each other both in the primary 5 sequence and the tertiary structure, facilitating such coordinated transitions. It should be noted that there is a loop to helical transition seen in the long BH of Cas9, which we have shown in our previous studies to possess an allosteric effect in DNA cleavage mechanism and RNA-DNA mismatch sensitivity (Babu et al., 2019, Babu et al., 2021 and Wu et al., 2025). Thus, while the BH’s helical transition and its allosteric effect on DNA cleavage seems to be a conserved mechanism in Cas9 and Cas12a, the structural features contributing to this allostery seem to be evolutionarily divergent. We have included these results and discussions in our revised manuscript [e.g., Results section, page 18 (lines 3-19), which is copied below]. “Structural overlays of the BH and RuvC domain (motifs I, II, and III) of Cas9 (subtypes II-A, II-B, and II- C) with those of FnoCas12a show that the BH and a helix of the RuvC motif-II of Cas9 have a similar structural arrangement to that in Cas12a. While helix in the RuvC motif-II of Cas9 and Cas12a RuvC- H1 shows a better structural overlay, the BH of Cas9 is prominently longer and does not align with that of FnoCas12a (Fig. 5b, Supplementary Fig. 22-23). Another significant difference between Cas9 and Cas12 is the insertion of the REC lobe between BH and RuvC motif-II, compared to their direct connection in Cas12 families (Supplementary Fig. 23). This long separation can potentially disrupt coordinated conformational changes between BH and RuvC-H1 that are present in Cas12s. Within the Cas9, there is a loop-to-helical transition of the BH in response to RNA binding that has been demonstrated to impact DNA cleavage efficiency and DNA mismatch sensitivity6,11,13,32,33,52. These observations show that while the fundamental mechanism of loop-to-helical transition of the BH is conserved in Cas12a and Cas9, the mechanisms for coordinated conformational changes differ between them. While the RuvC-H1 of RuvC motif-II is co-opted by Cas12 families to undergo coupled transformations with the BH to orchestrate conformational changes needed for assembling the pre- catalytic state, such coupling is absent in Cas9 (Supplementary Fig. 23c). Thus, nature seems to have optimized Cas12a and Cas9 molecular mechanisms differently to attain the same goal of RNA-directed, sequence-specific, DNA cleavage.” 4. Cas12a’s ability to recognize mismatches is only briefly mentioned. A more detailed discussion would be useful, especially given its implications for high-fidelity genome editing. We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. To address this, we have expanded the discussion to highlight prior biochemical evidence that demonstrated FnoCas12aKD2P’s RNA-DNA mismatch sensitivity that was reported in our previous work (Parameshwaran et al., 2021). Additionally, we 6 included two selected DNA mismatches (MM2 and MM13, representing PAM-proximal and PAM-middle DNA mismatch) to characterize the on-target vs. off-target cleavage effects of the new variants that were created during the revision of this manuscript. These data show that combining BH and RuvC-lid amino acid substitutions exacerbate mismatch sensitivity and provides both structural and biochemical support for a BH-dependent checkpoint that enforces the DNA cleavage fidelity of Cas12a. [Discussion section, page 20 (lines 5-26), which is copied below]. “In another role, the loop-to-helical transition of RuvC’s lid has been shown to play an important role in bringing the TS strand into the active site pocket for DNA cleavage21,27. The AsCas12a structures probing the TS strand entry mechanisms (PDB: 8SFP, 8SFQ and 8SFR21) also support these since the BH is extended towards the RNA-DNA hybrid, establishing interactions with the RuvC-lid helix, which leads to the exposure of the active site pocket in these structures. While we do not have structural features to support the TS entry mechanism due to the presence of partial DNA strands, BH’s helical transition appears to be critical in the passage and cleavage of the TS. This is supported by our previous work and biochemical assays reported in the present work. We observed a 6-fold reduction in TS compared to only a 3-fold reduction in NTS cleavage by FnoCas12aKD2P compared to that by FnoCas12aWT 14. Additionally, FnoCas12aKD2P discriminates the RNA-DNA mismatches by preventing TS cleavage since it was able to nick substrates with mismatches but not linearize them14. The efficiency to cleave mismatches is lower for all 20 nucleotides along the RNA-DNA hybrid, with mismatches at positions 12-17 of the target DNA producing higher accumulation of the nicked intermediate (61-77%) compared to that in FnoCas12aWT (3-19%)14. In this study, we observe that variants with disrupted BH–RuvC-lid interactions (R964A, E1020A/K1021A) in the FnoCas12aKD2P background exhibit pronounced reductions in cleavage of both TS and NTS, while the significant effect observed in FnoCas12aWT is the reduction in linearization and accumulation of nicked intermediate for MM13 substrate. Together, these results indicate that the BH’s loop-to-helical transition is the main driving force in R-loop propagation and the opening of the RuvC-lid in response to the total length of the RNA-DNA hybrid. Further studies are needed to find the mismatch-sensing mechanism of FnoCas12aKD2P, especially to understand why positions 12-18 of the RNA-DNA paired region is more sensitive compared to the rest of the R-loop positions.” Minor Comments 1. Suitability for Nature Communications 1. Given the structural focus of this manuscript, I would recommend publication in a more suitably specialized journal (i.e. Structure). This manuscript is purely focused on structural biology and, as such, would be a better fit for journals more so catered to this focus. To improve the suitability of our manuscript to Nature Communications, in the revision, we have added detailed biochemical and computational analyses as well as deepened our bioinformatics analysis to include a comparison between the BHs of Cas12 and Cas9 families. The results further strengthen the structural insights from the cryo-EM data and provide experimental evidence for RuvC–BH and BH–RNA/DNA interactions. Finally, the computational results establish a cooperativity between all the three components (BH, RuvC-lid, RNA-DNA hybrid) providing the first direct evidence of BH’s allosteric mechanism in organizing a DNA cleavage competent state of Cas12a. This highlights BH’s loop-to helical transition as the allosteric trigger needed to propagate R-loop beyond 15 nucleotides of pairing and the subsequent activation of Cas12a for DNA cleavage (i.e., loop to helical transition of RuvC-lid exposing the active site for DNA entry). Points have been added in the Results section, page 16 (lines 7-24), and Supplementary Methods 3, which has been shown in page 4 of the rebuttal to address Major Comment 1 of Reviewer #1, computational studies). Interestingly, our new analyses including Cas9 show that while there is a helix in the RuvC motif-II of Cas9 subtypes that is positioned in a similar arrangement as that of the RuvC-H1 of Cas12a’s RuvC-motif-II, the coordinated conformational changes between RuvC helix and BH is absent in apo, binary, and ternary structures of Cas9. The insertion of the large REC lobe between the BH and RuvC motif-II’s helix may deter such allostery between the BH and RuvC in Cas9. We point to our previous work on Cas9 BH’s conformational change that involves a loop-to-helical transition within the BH domain, alluding to the mechanistic similarities and structural differences of these divergent Cas proteins. Major Comments 2. The authors rightly bolster their results through comparison to similar structures in Stella et al., 2018, and Strohkendl et al., 2024, which describe conceptually similar findings focused on FnoCas12a and AsCas12a, respectively. However, it is unclear in this manuscript what is the new intellectual contribution 13 aside from the role of this mutated bridge helix. The manuscript would benefit from a clearer presentation of what is new. We thank the reviewer for this critical comment since that has helped us to differentiate our contributions and place them rightly among those from the previous literature. Here is a list of the main findings from our work and how it relates to previous literature. • The previous studies reported the structures of the wild-type (WT) Cas12a orthologs in several states. Our structures capture several conformational intermediates that are different than those that were captured in the previous work. These structures demonstrate how the inability of the BH’s loop-to-helical transition traps the protein in conformational intermediates compared to what was seen in WT under the normal conformational cascade. These structures directly connect the BH’s conformational change as a necessity for R-loop formation past the checkpoint (around 16 nucleotides), and how it is intimately related to RuvC-lid opening. The results also show that the structures of the BH-impaired variant are able to capture the earlier states (I1 to I3 of FnoCas12aWT) in the conformational cascade, but not the later ones, providing direct evidence that BH is an allosteric regulator for the conformational coordination towards the later stages of the activation process. Thus, while WT structures offer conformational changes needed for Cas12a activation, the importance of BH’s conformational change and its allosteric control is not discernible only by comparing the WT structures. • We also see slight differences in the BH’s conformational changes among the different orthologs. In FnoCas12a, the BH undergoes a loop-to-helical transition in response to R-loop propagation followed by the bending of the BH to latch onto the growing R-loop. However, in AsCas12a and LbCas12a, the BH remains elongated in the binary and the initial conformational states and bends toward the R-loop post 16 nucleotides of base pairing that is a conformational checkpoint in the activation process (Supplementary Fig. 24). Thus, the BH’s loop-to-helical transition in FnoCas12a appears to serve as an additional structural sensor for RNA-DNA hybrid propagation, melting of RuvC’s H1, and opening of RuvC-lid that are all needed for catalytic activation. • The functionally important W971 that inserts into the REC2 domain in the later stages of catalytic activation is the residue right adjacent to the BH, located in-between the BH and RuvC H1. Our structures show that an impaired loop-to-helical conformational change of the BH prevents 14 insertion of W971 to REC2’s hydrophobic pocket that implicates that proper REC2 docking is facilitated by BH’s conformational change. • We validated our structural findings through biochemical assays, which revealed that contacts between the BH and RuvC-lid (R964–E1020, E961–K1021) are only secondary to BH’s helical transition for orchestrating the conformational transitions required for double-strand cleavage and mismatch sensitivity. The wild-type protein with an intact conformational change in the BH is able to linearize (i.e., both NTS and TS cleavages) despite disrupting the BH-RuvC-lid interactions, with the only significant reduction being the second strand cleavage for MM13 substrate (Fig. 3e-f, Supplementary Figs. 17, 18, and Supplementary Table 11). Assessing mismatch sensitivity is also novel in this report compared to the previous work. • MD simulation results provide a mechanistic model for the structural and biochemical results. Correlation analyses reveal a reorganization of allosteric coupling between BH, RuvC-H1, and nucleic acids: from antagonistic DNA–crRNA interactions in S2, to DNA-dominated antagonism in S4b, and ultimately to strongly coordinated correlations with crRNA, DNA, RuvC-H1 and RuvC-lid in I4. Notably, this coordinated coupling is absent in the impaired BH variant, underscoring the requirement of BH’s loop-to-helical transition for establishing the allosteric network that licenses catalytic activation. To our knowledge, this is the first direct experimental and computational evidence implicating BH as the allosteric trigger to coordinate such diverse aspects (crRNA, DNA, REC2 docking, RuvC-H1 melting, and RuvC-lid opening) of the DNA cleavage competent state of Cas12a. • Alongside biochemical and computational analyses to investigate the role of bridge helix (BH) transitions in Cas12a activation, we also performed a comprehensive bioinformatics analysis to assess the structural conservation of BH–RuvC-helix 1 (H1) allosteric coupling across Cas12 and Cas9 protein families. We show conserved BH–RuvC-H1 mechanism in Cas12 subfamilies, while an absence of this coupling in Cas9 where REC lobe in inserted in between the BH and the RuvC helix. This, we believe, is the first report analyzing the similarities and differences of BH-mediated structural mechanisms of Cas9 and Cas12a. 15 3. Further, the two referenced manuscripts described above resolve structures of WT enzymes, whereas this manuscript focuses on a Cas12 variant with a modified bridge helix domain thought to slow kinetics of conformational transitions. While this mutant system may be descriptive of WT mechanisms, the lack of biochemical confirmation of their findings makes it challenging to distinguish if these lessons learned are broadly applicable or simply idiosyncrasies of an impaired system. To address this important point raised by the reviewer, we have added biochemical and MD simulation experiments in the revised manuscript. These results, along with the cryo-EM structures, demonstrate that the structural interactions that we identified are not idiosyncrasies, rather a potentially conserved mechanism in orthologs due to similar amino acids and conformational changes that are observed in the orthologs. Specifically: i. The BH arginines (e.g., R964 and R968 in FnoCas12a) are conserved (Supplementary Fig. 21) across Cas12a orthologs, which indicates that the interaction networks we describe, particularly those linking the BH and the RuvC-lid, are not specific to FnoCas12a but represent a general regulatory feature. ii. The biochemical experiments clearly demonstrate that BH’s loop-to-helical transition is the most important process in Cas12a’s activation rather than BH-RuvC interactions (please see details in the points for the previous comment). Our results implicate the following order of events in the activation process: BH’s helical transition, R-loop propagations past 16 nucleotides and REC2 docking by placement of W971 and opening of RuvC through BH-lid interactions. This clear distinction was possible through biochemical experiments that tested the variants with disrupted BH–RuvC-lid interactions in both FnoCas12aWT and FnoCas12aKD2P, as well as using matched and mismatched DNA substrates. Our results show that the impaired BH dynamics in FnoCas12aKD2P heighten mismatch sensitivity, reinforcing the fact that the BH’s conformational change is not only a checkpoint for activation for DNA cleavage but also a critical determinant of DNA cleavage fidelity, providing information that facilitate the improvement of gene editing accuracy. iii. MD simulation results show a shift in the correlated movements between BH–RuvC-H1, BH– RuvC-lid and BH–crRNA–DNA from anti-correlated to positively correlated interactions going from S2 to S4b to I4. This provides the first direct evidence of BH-mediated allostery in organizing the activated form of Cas12a for DNA cleavage. Together, these results show that, while the FnoCas12aKD2P variant allowed us to capture otherwise transient intermediates, the insights gained are not limited to this impaired system. Instead, the 16 combination of structural, biochemical, and computational analyses demonstrates that the BH’s helical transition and bending towards R-loop, RuvC-H1 melting, and BH–RuvC-lid interactions are general mechanistic features of Cas12a enzymes with direct implications on catalytic activation and RNA-DNA mismatch sensitivity. 4. While the authors have made efforts to biochemically characterize this specific mutant of FnoCas12a (Priya et al. 2021), and indeed some results from this previous manuscript strengthen claims made here, their previous work was largely focused on catalysis with little biochemical evidence to directly support the claims made in this manuscript which implicate the bridge helix in pre-catalysis conformational changes. More biochemistry is required here. We have addressed this concern by including biochemical characterization of several new variants that test the effect of interaction of BH and RuvC-lid residues in DNA cleavage mechanism. By comparing these variants in both FnoCas12aWT and FnoCas12aKD2P variant, our manuscript clearly establishes that the effect from BH’s helical transition and bending towards R-loop surpasses the requirement of BH–RuvC-lid interactions in orchestrating the changes needed for DNA cleavage (Figs. 3e-f, Supplementary Figs. 17, 18, and Supplementary Table 11). Please also see the detailed responses to the previous reviewer comments). 5. The figures in this manuscript are simplified to the point where it makes their interpretation challenging. Figures containing protein structures are under-labeled and stripped of context, requiring frequent reference to the manuscript, figure legend, and occasionally the provided structures, to properly understand. Increased labeling (as seen in figure 5B) and structural context callouts (as seen in figure 2A) would go a long way in increasing the clarity of the images to the reader. We appreciate the reviewer’s comment regarding figure clarity. To make the figures self-explanatory, we have revised the figures by: • Standardizing the color scheme for protein domains and RNA-DNA elements across all figures to minimize the need for cross-referencing • Adding labels and structural callouts (residues, domains, and regions of interest) to provide context within each panel • Including informative annotations within the figures themselves to highlight key conformational changes to reduce the reliance on figure legends 17 We believe that these changes will enable the figures to stand alone and improve readability. Minor Comments • The authors note on page 17 that their enzyme FnoCas12aKD2P is unable to perform trans-cleavage. Priya et al. 2021 demonstrates that while trans-cleavage is dramatically inhibited in FnoCas12aKD2P it does still occur if incubated for long enough – at least with M13 ssDNA. We appreciate the reviewer pointing out this discrepancy. We have reworded the text to clarify this by including discussion on data points from the previous publication. (Discussion section, page 21, lines 1-9, which is copied below). “In our previous work, we have also demonstrated that FnoCas12aKD2P has a lower trans-cleavage efficiency (0% substrate left for FnoCas12aWT at 5 minutes, compared to 40% remaining in FnoCas12aKD2P after two hours)14. Unlike FnoCas12aWT, which rapidly degraded substrates, FnoCas12aKD2P accumulated linear intermediates and failed to sustain a robust progressive trans-cleavage14. Additionally, FnoCas12aKD2P was unable to perform trans-cleavage when activated by a dsDNA14. The trans-cleavage occurs through keeping the RuvC domain “open” for non-specific ssDNA to access the active site24,53. These observations highlight that impairment of the BH’s helical transition likely blocks the prolonged activated form of the RuvC pocket, preventing trans-cleavage in FnoCas12aKD2P.” • While the bioinformatics was well done, I thought that, in line with my comments above, the associated figures highlighting structural similarities were unclear (though these were much better than previous figures). Further, the commentary on the bioinformatics portion of this manuscript was surface level and somewhat vague with little discussion beyond how they are structurally (and thus potentially mechanistically) similar. We suggest that the implications of this bioinformatic analysis be explored in the discussion section. For example, how frequently do these domain insertions occur across similar systems? We appreciate the reviewer's feedback on the bioinformatics analysis and figures. We performed further analysis by including the available structures of Cas9 subtypes (II-A, II-B and II-C) in our previous pairwise 3D structural comparison of the BH-RuvC domain of FnoCas12a and various Cas12 subtypes. This enabled us to make important observations regarding both the structural and mechanistic similarities and differences in the BH–RuvC-H1 regions of Cas12 subtypes as well as between Cas12 18 and Cas9 proteins. We have discussed differences in the primary and structural arrangement of Cas9 and Cas12 RuvC domain and how these structural arrangements are implicated in their conformational changes. We have also remade the figures highlighting structural similarities (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Figs. 22 and 23) for more clarity and have also included appropriate figures for the additional information on Cas9. • We found typos/grammatical errors in the manuscript, please proofread carefully. We appreciate the reviewer’s feedback and have conducted a thorough proofreading to ensure accuracy and clarity before submitting the revised version. Reviewer #4 and co-reviewer #5 Comments: The molecular dynamics (MD) simulations complement the experimental structures by examining the conformational behavior of Cas12a across several experimentally defined functional states. The study focuses on how the bridge helix (BH) transition from a loop to a helix may contribute to the enzyme’s activation mechanism. The authors simulated four states: wild-type (I2 and I4) and mutant (S2 and S4b), each for 1 μs. Principal component analysis (PCA) revealed distinct conformational clusters for each state, which the authors interpret as a progression from early (S2/I2) to pre-catalytic (I4) conformations, with S4b representing an intermediate. Cross-correlation analyses were further used to probe potential allosteric coupling between the BH, RuvC-H1, RuvC-lid, and nucleic acids. According to the authors, these correlations become stronger in the active state, whereas the KD2P mutant shows disrupted and anti-correlated motions, which they propose explains its reduced catalytic efficiency. The molecular dynamics (MD) component of this study provides valuable mechanistic context to the experimental findings by exploring the conformational dynamics of Cas12a in different functional states. Overall, the MD protocol appears well-designed and appropriately detailed. The selection of trajectories and analyses is well aligned with the study’s stated goals. However, several points related to clarity, consistency, and methodological transparency could be improved to further strengthen the computational section. We thank the reviewers for the positive comments on how the MD simulations complement the structural and functional studies and help us solidify the molecular mechanisms. Below we list revisions that were made to improve clarity, consistency, and methodological transparency. Comment 1: The description of the cross-correlation analysis lacks sufficient methodological detail. It is not clear which software, module, or specific algorithm was used to compute the correlation matrices (e.g., CPPTRAJ, Bio3D, or an in-house script). 1 The reference frame, atom selection, and specific trajectory segments used for this analysis should also be specified for reproducibility. Additionally, it is not mentioned which frames of the MD trajectories were analyzed. Since the initial part of the simulation often represents equilibration rather than equilibrium dynamics, clarification is needed on whether only equilibrated frames (e.g., after RMSD or energy stabilization) were included, which is standard practice. This information is important to ensure that the reported correlations reflect genuine conformational dynamics rather than transient relaxation artifacts. Response 1: We thank the reviewers for the comment. We have modified the following paragraphs to provide more information on the MD analysis and to clarify our workflow. Specifically, in Supplemental Methods 3 (page S9, line 33 to page S10, line 6) and added Supplementary Figure 19 (page S41), we added a description of our use of CPPTRAJ, reference frame, atom selection, and trajectory segments in the cross-correlation analysis: “Cross-correlation analyses using CPPTRAJ were performed to delineate the allosteric control of BH’s loop-to-helical transition in other regions of the protein (RuvC-H1 and RuvC-lid) as well as with crRNA and DNA. As the RMSD values (Supplementary Fig. 19) indicated, all systems were equilibrated after 100 ns of MD simulation, which was further supported by the PCA analysis showing compact clusters for each trajectory (Supplementary Fig. 20). For the cross-correlation analysis, the reference was chosen to be the average structure of each MD simulation, and all carbon atoms of the protein along with the phosphorous atoms of the DNA/RNA were included in the analysis. The cross-correlation matrix was constructed using the last 900 ns of the MD trajectory, excluding the first 100 ns of equilibration.” Supplementary Figure 19: Root Mean Square Deviation (RMSD) of the simulation trajectory of FnoCas12aWT and FnoCas12aKD2P states. Colored lines represent the individual states: FnoCas12aKD2P-S2 (purple) and FnoCas12aKD2P-S4b (green) of FnoCas12aKD2P, and FnoCas12aWT-I2 (blue) and FnoCas12aWT-I4 (orange). The RMSDs were calculated by comparing each frame of the 1 μs MD trajectory to the initial structure of each system. 2 To further demonstrate the sampling convergence, below we color the PCA cluster for each system that is shown in Supplemental Figure 20a by the simulation time (ranging from blue to red as the simulation time increases). Fig. R1. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) of the simulation trajectories of FnoCas12aKD2P and FnoCas12aWT states. The analysis was performed on a total of 4 μs of concatenated MD trajectories comprising all four states. The color starts from blue and ends with red for each 1 μs trajectory. In the Methods section of the main text, we also added (page 29, lines 8-12): “Each system underwent 1 μs NVT simulation. The resulting trajectories, totaling 4 μs after including all the systems, were concatenated and analyzed using Principal Component Analysis (PCA). For the cross-correlation analysis, the first 100 ns of equilibration was excluded and only the last 900 ns of each trajectory were used. Both PCA and cross-correlation analyses were performed using CPPTRAJ⁶⁶.” Comment 2: In interpreting correlation results, correlation should not be equated with direct physical interaction. Statements such as “interaction network”, 'I4 state shows strong interactions with A3', and "Lid also supports DNA positioning in I4" could be softened to emphasize changes in correlated motion rather than binding. Response 2: We thank the reviewers for this comment. We have revised the text accordingly (Supplementary Methods 3, page S10, line 15-35): “Also, FnoCas12aKD2P-S4b displays a partial breakdown of this correlated motion network, with the emergence of a new network hotspot involving residues around 969 in BH–RuvC-H1 and 1017-1021 in RuvC-lid, indicating a possible structural rearrangement. These shifts suggest a progressive reorganization of the BH–RuvC-H1– RuvC-lid correlated motion network across the activation cycle. While FnoCas12aKD2P- S2 shows fewer contacts between these elements, FnoCas12aKD2P-S4b exhibits a noticeable increase, and FnoCas12aWT-I4 displays the most extensive correlated motion 3 network (Supplementary Fig. 21a). This trend indicates that FnoCas12aKD2P-S4b may represent a transitional state, where the coupling between BH–RuvC-H1 and the RuvC- lid is beginning to resemble that of the fully activated FnoCas12aWT-I4. Such a redistribution of contacts likely reflects functional remodeling and supports the idea that RuvC-lid engagement is strengthened as the complex progresses towards activation. The matrix cross-correlation analysis also shows a shift in the coordinated motions of RuvC-lid–crRNA in states S2 to S4b of FnoCas12aKD2P (Supplementary Fig. 21b). This is indicated by the absence of correlations (up to 0.44) between the RuvC-lid and crRNA in FnoCas12aKD2P-S2, highlighting that RuvC-lid is not coupled to crRNA positioning in this state (Supplementary Table 15). In FnoCas12aKD2P-S4b, the RuvC- lid–crRNA correlations become stronger (up to 0.46), with even more stronger correlations (over 0.55) for BH–RuvC-H1–crRNA as highlighted by residues 961-985 with A1 and G2 of crRNA (Supplementary Table 16). This suggests that BH–RuvC-H1 takes over crRNA coupling, pointing to a conformational shift in how the protein stabilizes the crRNA. In comparison, FnoCas12aWT-I44 shows strongly correlated motions of G5, U6, C7, and A8 of crRNA with residues in both RuvC-lid and BH–RuvC-H1 regions (Supplementary Table 17).” Comment 3: Consistency in the labeling of simulation states would improve readability. Throughout the MD section, state identifiers alternate between full notation (e.g., FnoCas12aKD2P–S2/S4 and FnoCas12aWT–I2/I4) and abbreviated forms (S2/S4, I2/I4). Standardizing this nomenclature across the text and figures would enhance clarity. Response 3: To address this, we have revised the MD section to match with the rest of the manuscript to ensure consistency in our nomenclature for the states. We have kept the protein name along with the specific state when we are referring to a selected structure. When we are referring to S2, S4b, and I4 as different conformational states towards reaching the activated complex, we have not used the protein name to give emphasis on the conformational state irrespective of the specific protein. Comment 4: Correlation values are not crystal clear in Fig. 4 and Fig. SF20. It is stated in the captions that “Correlation values range from +1 (red) to -1 (blue), with a visual cutoff applied for values above 0.4 and below -0.4 to enhance clarity”. This would normally be interpreted as the existence of a range of colors (and values) between red and blue, but as a matter of fact only red and blue are shown, no intermediate colors/values. The correlation values in the correlation plots (Fig. 4 and Supplementary Fig. 20) indeed ranges from +1 (red) to -1 (blue), with 0 (white) representing no correlation. The color intensity reflects the strength of the correlation, where saturated red or blue corresponds to the most positive or negative correlation, respectively. The correlations at the value of 0.4 appear as pink and -0.4 as light blue. Weaker correlations, with values above -0.4 and below 0.4, are not displayed in these plots. 4 We tried using another color other than white to represent the non-correlated values; however, adding another color made it difficult to understand the scheme. To enhance clarity, we have added a color bar and updated Figures 4c-e and Supplementary Figure 21 (page S43). Figure 4. reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
We thank all the reviewers for their positive feedback about the significance of the work and their critical comments that have greatly helped us improve the quality of our manuscript and distinguish the contributions of this manuscript over the previously existing literature. A point-by-point response to the reviewer comments is below in blue.
REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
This manuscript provides a detailed structural analysis of the bridge helix (BH) in Cas12a activation, offering insights into its role in allosteric regulation. The cryoEM data are well-analyzed, and the findings contribute meaningfully to the understanding of Cas12a’s conformational transitions. The study is of interest to researchers in CRISPR biology and genome editing. While the manuscript is generally well-prepared, some points require further clarification and discussion to strengthen the conclusions.
We thank the reviewer for the positive feedback about the significance of the work and the quality of cryo-EM data analysis and its contribution to understanding the role of BH in Cas12a’s activation. Points which needed further clarification are addressed in the revision as described below.
Major Comments
1. The study suggests that BH’s loop-to-helical transition directly influences RuvC activation. However, it remains unclear whether this is a cause or a consequence of R-loop formation. Additional discussion, or reference to supporting biochemical evidence, would help clarify this point.
To clarify whether BH’s loop-to-helical transition is a cause or a consequence of R-loop formation and its influence on RuvC activation, we have conducted additional biochemical, structural, and computational analyzes. The results now clearly establish that BH’s loop-to-helical transition is a cause since without this transition, R-loop formation is inhibited mid-way through, and the formation of the helical structure of the hybrid is impaired. We also show that, with a variant able to undergo the loop-to-helical transition, BH–RuvC-lid interactions are only secondary as the variants maintain efficient on-target DNA cleavage without the BH–RuvC-lid interactions.
1
Biochemical Analysis:
To probe the allosteric mechanism, residues that mediate BH-lid interactions to convert the lid from a loop to a helical form at different stages of the activation process, thereby mediating the exposure of RuvC active site, were identified based on wild-type (FnoCas12aWT) and BH-variant (FnoCas12aKD2P) structures. Residues R964 of the BH and E1020 and K1021 of the RuvC-lid were substituted with alanine, along with a double variant E1020A/K1021A in both FnoCas12aWT and FnoCas12aKD2P backgrounds. In vitro plasmid DNA cleavage assays using both matched (MCH) and mismatched (MM) DNA substrates (MM2, PAM proximal mismatch and MM13, mid R-loop mismatch) were performed to assess the effects of the alanine substitutions. In the FnoCas12aWT background, single substitutions do not show prominent impairments, except for MM13-R964A combination, consistent with the stabilizing effect that the BH offers for the allosteric interactions. On the other hand, in the FnoCas12aKD2P background, where BH stability is impaired by the proline substitutions, the substitutions at R964 of the BH and the double variant (E1020/K1021) of the RuvC-lid, impacted both TS and NTS cleavages. In comparison, the only significant impact seen in FnoCas12aWT is the accumulation of nicked intermediate in R964A-MM13 combination (Figures 3e-f, Supplementary Figs.17,18, and Supplementary Table 11). These data clearly show that DNA cleavage is an additive process with combinations from effects from the BH’s loop-to-helical transition, opening of the RuvC active site by the helical transition of the lid, and the strength of complementary pairing between the RNA and DNA. Of these three, BH’s transition has the most significant contribution since in the wild-type backbone, all substitutions show minimal effect, except in R964-MM13, which indicates that the second contributor is the strength of complementary base pairing that is also dictated by the position of the mismatch between the RNA and DNA. The new results are presented in pages 12-15, with a summary in pages 14 (lines 23-26, and 15 (lines 1-10) which is copied below.
“Our findings show that contacts between the BH and RuvC-lid (R964-E1020, E961-K1021) are only secondary to the BH’s helical transition for orchestrating the conformational transitions required for double-strand cleavage and mismatch sensitivity. The wild-type protein with an intact conformational change in the BH can linearize (i.e., both NTS and TS cleavages) despite disrupting the BH–RuvC-lid interactions, with the only significant reduction being in the second strand cleavage for MM13 substrate (Supplementary Fig. 17 and Supplementary Table 11). On the contrary, when BH’s sturdiness is restricted, as in the FnoCas12aKD2P variant, the enzyme becomes highly dependent on these interactions to provide RuvC active site access to ssDNA. In the FnoCas12aKD2P background, while R964A and E1020A/K1021A substitutions impair both strand cleavages, single substitutions (E1020A or K1021A) impede second-strand cleavage (Supplementary Fig. 18a and Supplementary Table 11). These
2
results demonstrate that the BH’s loop-to-helical transition is an allosteric switch coupling R-loop propagation to catalysis and point to the importance of the helicity of the BH in assisting the passage of TS DNA into the RuvC active site pocket. BH, RuvC-H1, and RuvC-lid are potential engineering sites to reduce mismatch tolerance in Cas12a.”
Structural Analysis:
Structural analysis showed that R964 and R968 interact with nucleotides dG(-7), dT(-8), and U10 of crRNA/DNA in state I4 of FnoCas12aWT (Supplementary Fig.15), while the corresponding interaction is absent in FnoCas12aKD2P (a maximum of 11 base pairs is visible in State 4a). While position 11 of crRNA and TS DNA move closer to the BH in FnoCas12aWT, this interaction stays at around 20 Å FnoCas12aKD2P. Previous studies have shown that 16 nucleotides of base pairing of crRNA and DNA is a checkpoint for Cas12a activation (Stella et al., 2018 and Strohkendl et al., 2024). Thus, it appears that BH’s transition is essential for R-loop propagation, making BH’s transition the cause for R-loop propagation, especially past 10-nucleotides of base pairing. The bending of BH towards R-loop and latching into REC2 domain in parallel with the growing RNA-DNA hybrid appears to give the RNA-DNA hybrid a double-helical structure, implicating the importance of BH in R-loop propagation and stability. This stable configuration of the BH and the R-loop seems to facilitate a concomitant opening of the RuvC active pocket through RuvC-lid remodeling. These points have been added to the Discussion section (page 19 (lines 14-26), which is copied below).
“In addition, the elongation of the BH due to the addition of the new helical turns and its bending towards the RNA-DNA hybrid appears to be critical in providing an anchorage for R-loop and to complete the RNA-DNA hybrid formation. In the FnoCas12aWT structures, states I2 and I320 have BH in a loop state prior to its the helical conversion. In these structures, BH is at a distance of 17 Å from the RNA-DNA hybrid with a total of 8-nucleotides of base pairing between the crRNA-guide and TS DNA. In comparison, in state I4, we see a fully formed and bent BH that is closer to the RNA-DNA hybrid (6 Å). In FnoCas12aKD2P, which is not capable of undergoing the loop-to-helical transition, we only see up to a maximum of 11-nucleotides of base pairing between the crRNA-guide and TS DNA, with a distance of ~20 Å from the BH. Interestingly, we also see stacking and distortion of bases towards the end of the R-loop, implicating that the strands are not aligned well with an impaired BH, hinting at the essentiality of the stability provided by the BH in these intermediary stages to drive R-loop propagation. The slowing down of the structural transitions is supported by the lower reaction kinetics of FnoCas12aKD2P when compared to FnoCas12aWT14..”

Computational Studies:
⁠Our MD simulations indicate that the BH’s loop-to-helical transition actively shapes the conformational landscape of Cas12a by exerting allosteric influence over the RuvC-lid, crRNA, and DNA. Cross-correlation analyses show a shift from anti-correlated to positively correlated interactions across states, such as S2 to S4b to I4 (especially for nucleotides at position 6 and 8 of crRNA and -8 to -4 of DNA). This reorganization coincides only with the helical transition of the BH, which in turn facilitates the emergence of strong BH–crRNA, BH–DNA, and BH–RuvC-lid couplings in the pre-catalytic state. Overall, these data show that BH’s helical transition is an activating trigger regulating R-loop propagation and opening of RuvC active site pocket (Points have been added in the Results section, page 16 (lines 8-24), which is copied below, and Supplementary Methods 3).
“To delineate potential allosteric communication between BH and nucleic acid, we performed correlation analyses of the residues E961, R964, R968, K981, E1020, K1021, and N1022 of the BH, RuvC-H1, and RuvC-lid, as well as nucleotides in crRNA and DNA (Fig. 4c-e). The complete correlation analysis is available in Supplementary Methods 3. Results reveal that BH–RuvC-H1 and RuvC-lid conformations exhibit strongly correlated motions with those of the crRNA and DNA, and that the motions are different between the different states. FnoCas12aKD2P S2 has fewer correlated motions (i.e., components move in the same direction) between the BH–RuvC-H1 and RuvC-lid, while there are several anti-correlated motions (i.e., components move in the opposite direction) between BH–RuvC-H1 and the RNA and DNA (Fig. 4c). In the intermediate state S4b, however, this correlation pattern shifts; there is an increase in the correlated motions between BH–RuvC-H1 and RuvC-lid and a few new motions with the crRNA, while there still is a substantial number of anti-correlated motions with crRNA and DNA (Fig. 4d). In I420 of FnoCas12aWT, we see only correlated motions between BH–RuvC-H1, RuvC-lid, crRNA, and DNA (Fig. 4e). Interestingly, some of the interactions with crRNA and DNA include nucleotides near the middle of the R-loop (~8) providing mechanistic clues on why mismatches between the crRNA and DNA in the R-loop away from the PAM are particularly sensitive in FnoCas12a. This reorganization of the correlation network in different states of the protein points to the pivotal role that the BH–RuvC-H1 transitions play in organizing the cleavage-competent form of Cas12a.”

We thank the reviewer for this critical comment since that has helped us to differentiate our contributions and place them rightly among those from the previous literature. Here is a list of the main findings from our work and how it relates to previous literature.
• The previous studies reported the structures of the wild-type (WT) Cas12a orthologs in several states. Our structures capture several conformational intermediates that are different than those that were captured in the previous work. These structures demonstrate how the inability of the BH’s loop-to-helical transition traps the protein in conformational intermediates compared to what was seen in WT under the normal conformational cascade. These structures directly connect the BH’s conformational change as a necessity for R-loop formation past the checkpoint (around 16 nucleotides), and how it is intimately related to RuvC-lid opening. The results also show that the structures of the BH-impaired variant are able to capture the earlier states (I1 to I3 of FnoCas12aWT) in the conformational cascade, but not the later ones, providing direct evidence that BH is an allosteric regulator for the conformational coordination towards the later stages of the activation process. Thus, while WT structures offer conformational changes needed for Cas12a activation, the importance of BH’s conformational change and its allosteric control is not discernible only by comparing the WT structures.
• We also see slight differences in the BH’s conformational changes among the different orthologs. In FnoCas12a, the BH undergoes a loop-to-helical transition in response to R-loop propagation followed by the bending of the BH to latch onto the growing R-loop. However, in AsCas12a and LbCas12a, the BH remains elongated in the binary and the initial conformational states and bends toward the R-loop post 16 nucleotides of base pairing that is a conformational checkpoint in the activation process (Supplementary Fig. 24). Thus, the BH’s loop-to-helical transition in FnoCas12a appears to serve as an additional structural sensor for RNA-DNA hybrid propagation, melting of RuvC’s H1, and opening of RuvC-lid that are all needed for catalytic activation.
• The functionally important W971 that inserts into the REC2 domain in the later stages of catalytic activation is the residue right adjacent to the BH, located in-between the BH and RuvC H1. Our structures show that an impaired loop-to-helical conformational change of the BH prevents
14
insertion of W971 to REC2’s hydrophobic pocket that implicates that proper REC2 docking is facilitated by BH’s conformational change.
• We validated our structural findings through biochemical assays, which revealed that contacts between the BH and RuvC-lid (R964–E1020, E961–K1021) are only secondary to BH’s helical transition for orchestrating the conformational transitions required for double-strand cleavage and mismatch sensitivity. The wild-type protein with an intact conformational change in the BH is able to linearize (i.e., both NTS and TS cleavages) despite disrupting the BH-RuvC-lid interactions, with the only significant reduction being the second strand cleavage for MM13 substrate (Supplementary Fig. 17 and Supplementary Table 11). On the contrary, with an impaired BH, disrupting the BH–RuvC-lid interactions exacerbate the DNA cleavage deficiency in FnoCas12aKD2P backbone (Fig. 3e-f, Supplementary Figs. 17, 18, and Supplementary Table 11). Assessing mismatch sensitivity is also novel in this report compared to the previous work.
• MD simulation results provide a mechanistic model for the structural and biochemical results. Correlation analyses reveal a reorganization of allosteric coupling between BH, RuvC-H1, and nucleic acids: from antagonistic DNA–crRNA interactions in S2, to DNA-dominated antagonism in S4b, and ultimately to strongly coordinated correlations with crRNA, DNA, RuvC-H1 and RuvC-lid in I4. Notably, this coordinated coupling is absent in the impaired BH variant, underscoring the requirement of BH’s loop-to-helical transition for establishing the allosteric network that licenses catalytic activation. To our knowledge, this is the first direct experimental and computational evidence implicating BH as the allosteric trigger to coordinate such diverse aspects (crRNA, DNA, REC2 docking, RuvC-H1 melting, and RuvC-lid opening) of the DNA cleavage competent state of Cas12a.
• Alongside biochemical and computational analyses to investigate the role of bridge helix (BH) transitions in Cas12a activation, we also performed a comprehensive bioinformatics analysis to assess the structural conservation of BH–RuvC-helix 1 (H1) allosteric coupling across Cas12 and Cas9 protein families. We show conserved BH–RuvC-H1 mechanism in Cas12 subfamilies, while an absence of this coupling in Cas9 where REC lobe in inserted in between the BH and the RuvC helix. This, we believe, is the first report analyzing the similarities and differences of BH-mediated structural mechanisms of Cas9 and Cas12a.

To address this important point raised by the reviewer, we have added biochemical and MD simulation experiments in the revised manuscript. These results, along with the cryo-EM structures, demonstrate that the structural interactions that we identified are not idiosyncrasies, rather a potentially conserved mechanism in orthologs due to similar amino acids and conformational changes that are observed in the orthologs. Specifically:
i. The BH arginines (e.g., R964 and R968 in FnoCas12a) are conserved (Supplementary Fig. 21) across Cas12a orthologs, which indicates that the interaction networks we describe, particularly those linking the BH and the RuvC-lid, are not specific to FnoCas12a but represent a general regulatory feature.
ii. The biochemical experiments clearly demonstrate that BH’s loop-to-helical transition is the most important process in Cas12a’s activation rather than BH-RuvC interactions (please see details in the points for the previous comment). Our results implicate the following order of events in the activation process: BH’s helical transition, R-loop propagations past 16 nucleotides and REC2 docking by placement of W971 and opening of RuvC through BH-lid interactions. This clear distinction was possible through biochemical experiments that tested the variants with disrupted BH–RuvC-lid interactions in both FnoCas12aWT and FnoCas12aKD2P, as well as using matched and mismatched DNA substrates. Our results show that the impaired BH dynamics in FnoCas12aKD2P heighten mismatch sensitivity, reinforcing the fact that the BH’s conformational change is not only a checkpoint for activation for DNA cleavage but also a critical determinant of DNA cleavage fidelity, providing information that facilitate the improvement of gene editing accuracy.
iii. MD simulation results show a shift in the correlated movements between BH–RuvC-H1, BH–RuvC-lid and BH–crRNA–DNA from anti-correlated to positively correlated interactions going from S2 to S4b to I4. This provides the first direct evidence of BH-mediated allostery in organizing the activated form of Cas12a for DNA cleavage.
Together, these results show that, while the FnoCas12aKD2P variant allowed us to capture otherwise transient intermediates, the insights gained are not limited to this impaired system. Instead, the
16
combination of structural, biochemical, and computational analyses demonstrates that the BH’s helical transition and bending towards R-loop, RuvC-H1 melting, and BH–RuvC-lid interactions are general mechanistic features of Cas12a enzymes with direct implications on catalytic activation and RNA-DNA mismatch sensitivity.
4. While the authors have made efforts to biochemically characterize this specific mutant of FnoCas12a (Priya et al. 2021), and indeed some results from this previous manuscript strengthen claims made here, their previous work was largely focused on catalysis with little biochemical evidence to directly support the claims made in this manuscript which implicate the bridge helix in pre-catalysis conformational changes. More biochemistry is required here.
We have addressed this concern by including biochemical characterization of several new variants that test the effect of interaction of BH and RuvC-lid residues in DNA cleavage mechanism. By comparing these variants in both FnoCas12aWT and FnoCas12aKD2P variant, our manuscript clearly establishes that the effect from BH’s helical transition and bending towards R-loop surpasses the requirement of BH–RuvC-lid interactions in orchestrating the changes needed for DNA cleavage (Figs. 3e-f, Supplementary Figs. 17, 18, and Supplementary Table 11). Please also see the detailed responses to the previous reviewer comments).
5. The figures in this manuscript are simplified to the point where it makes their interpretation challenging. Figures containing protein structures are under-labeled and stripped of context, requiring frequent reference to the manuscript, figure legend, and occasionally the provided structures, to properly understand. Increased labeling (as seen in figure 5B) and structural context callouts (as seen in figure 2A) would go a long way in increasing the clarity of the images to the reader.
We appreciate the reviewer’s comment regarding figure clarity. To make the figures self-explanatory, we have revised the figures by:
• Standardizing the color scheme for protein domains and RNA-DNA elements across all figures to minimize the need for cross-referencing
• Adding labels and structural callouts (residues, domains, and regions of interest) to provide context within each panel
• Including informative annotations within the figures themselves to highlight key conformational
changes to reduce the reliance on figure legends
17
We believe that these changes will enable the figures to stand alone and improve readability.
Minor Comments
• The authors note on page 17 that their enzyme FnoCas12aKD2P is unable to perform trans-cleavage. Priya et al. 2021 demonstrates that while trans-cleavage is dramatically inhibited in FnoCas12aKD2P it does still occur if incubated for long enough – at least with M13 ssDNA.
We appreciate the reviewer pointing out this discrepancy. We have reworded the text to clarify this by including discussion on data points from the previous publication. (Discussion section, page 21, lines 1-9, which is copied below).
“In our previous work, we have also demonstrated that FnoCas12aKD2P has a lower trans-cleavage efficiency (0% substrate left for FnoCas12aWT at 5 minutes, compared to 40% remaining in FnoCas12aKD2P after two hours)14. Unlike FnoCas12aWT, which rapidly degraded substrates, FnoCas12aKD2P accumulated linear intermediates and failed to sustain a robust progressive trans-cleavage14. Additionally, FnoCas12aKD2P was unable to perform trans-cleavage when activated by a dsDNA14. The trans-cleavage occurs through keeping the RuvC domain “open” for non-specific ssDNA to access the active site24,53. These observations highlight that impairment of the BH’s helical transition likely blocks the prolonged activated form of the RuvC pocket, preventing trans-cleavage in FnoCas12aKD2P.”
• While the bioinformatics was well done, I thought that, in line with my comments above, the associated figures highlighting structural similarities were unclear (though these were much better than previous figures). Further, the commentary on the bioinformatics portion of this manuscript was surface level and somewhat vague with little discussion beyond how they are structurally (and thus potentially mechanistically) similar. We suggest that the implications of this bioinformatic analysis be explored in the discussion section. For example, how frequently do these domain insertions occur across similar systems?
We appreciate the reviewer's feedback on the bioinformatics analysis and figures. We performed further analysis by including the available structures of Cas9 subtypes (II-A, II-B and II-C) in our previous pairwise 3D structural comparison of the BH-RuvC domain of FnoCas12a and various Cas12 subtypes. This enabled us to make important observations regarding both the structural and mechanistic similarities and differences in the BH–RuvC-H1 regions of Cas12 subtypes as well as between Cas12
18
and Cas9 proteins. We have discussed differences in the primary and structural arrangement of Cas9 and Cas12 RuvC domain and how these structural arrangements are implicated in their conformational changes. We have also remade the figures highlighting structural similarities (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Figs. 22 and 23) for more clarity and have also included appropriate figures for the additional information on Cas9.
• We found typos/grammatical errors in the manuscript, please proofread carefully.
We appreciate the reviewer’s feedback and have conducted a thorough proofreading to ensure accuracy and clarity before submitting the revised version.

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.
We thank reviewer 3 for their assistance in the review process.
19
We thank the reviewers for their insightful comments, which were helpful in increasing

Reviewer #1:
The authors have satisfactorily addressed all my previous comments. The revised
manuscript is clearly improved in both presentation and data interpretation. The
additional experiments and clarifications have strengthened the conclusions, and the

I have no further concerns.
We thank the reviewer for this feedback and are excited that the added experiments and

Comments:
The molecular dynamics (MD) simulations complement the experimental structures by
examining the conformational behavior of Cas12a across several experimentally defined
functional states. The study focuses on how the bridge helix (BH) transition from a loop
to a helix may contribute to the enzyme’s activation mechanism. The authors simulated

The molecular dynamics (MD) component of this study provides valuable mechanistic

We thank the reviewers for the positive comments on how the MD simulations

Comment 1: The description of the cross-correlation analysis lacks sufficient

1
